case_study_insert.main_stem: Meridian Print Works (MPW) is a public limited company in the commercial printing sector, employing a workforce of 90. Founded in 1998 by the printer Rowan Ashworth, it prints packaging and marketing material for national clients and runs a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. MPW plans to invest $900,000 in a digital printing press, financed by a $600,000 share issue and a $300,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $3.80 a unit and a selling price of $7.30, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. MPW faces paper waste of 5.4% and reprint complaints that have strained its quality control with national clients.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The print hall delivered 28,500 jobs last quarter with a defect rate of 2.0%, down from 3.6% a year earlier. Reprint complaints fell from 63 to 30 per month and paper waste was 5.4% of sheets used. Average turnaround is 4.3 days. A survey of 520 marketing managers found 71% value fast digital turnaround and 57% would pay $0.25 more per unit. A skills audit shows 22 of 90 press operators need digital-press training; courses cost $480 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Meridian Print Works as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.80%, raising borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage increases by 6.0% from $12.60 to $13.36 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale paper and ink input costs rose 10.2% year-on-year, while commercial printing demand grew 3.3%.

questions.question_text: MPW plans to raise $600,000 through a share issue for its $900,000 press. Explain two advantages for MPW of a share issue over increasing its $300,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue raises $600,000 of permanent capital with no interest charge and no fixed repayment schedule, unlike the $300,000 bank loan. With fixed costs of $300,000 a year, avoiding extra interest protects the $3.50 contribution on each of the 120,000 units and leaves cash to tackle the 5.4% paper waste. A rise in the base rate from 4.00% to 4.80% also cannot increase the cost of equity.

Point 2: Equity is not secured on MPW's assets, so the press cannot be repossessed if digital demand disappoints, and a public limited company can reach many investors. The $600,000 arrives in one amount, letting Rowan Ashworth install the $900,000 press at once to meet the 71% of 520 managers who value fast digital turnaround, rather than waiting for further loan tranches that a bank might refuse.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to MPW, its $900,000 press and its financing.

questions.question_text: MPW wants to reduce reprint complaints, now 30 a month. Consider end-of-line inspection, a quality assurance programme, or automating the press with the new digital machine. Which should MPW choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
End-of-line inspection: Checking finished jobs would catch the 2.0% defect rate before delivery and cut the 30 reprint complaints. It is easy to add to the 28,500 jobs handled last quarter. But inspection finds errors only after paper and ink have been used, so the 5.4% paper waste is already incurred; with 90 press operators, extra inspectors add cost to a firm funding a $900,000 press.

Quality assurance programme: Building quality into each stage, with operator checks and root-cause reviews, prevents errors rather than detecting them, attacking both the 2.0% defect rate and the fall from 63 to 30 complaints. It engages the 22 operators needing digital-press training and suits the 4.3-day turnaround. It takes time to embed and needs training investment before results appear, and the hierarchical structure may slow feedback from operators to managers.

Automation with the new digital press: The $900,000 digital press can reduce manual setup errors and shorten the 4.3-day turnaround, which 71% of 520 managers value. It can also cut reprints sharply once staff are trained. The capital cost is high, 22 operators need $480 training, and automation cannot fix poor artwork supplied by clients, which may be a source of the complaints.

Recommendation: MPW should choose the quality assurance programme. It prevents the 5.4% waste and reprints at source and complements the new digital press, whereas inspection only detects faults after cost is incurred and automation alone cannot solve client-artwork errors. Inspection can be kept as a backstop and the press will deliver speed, but the lasting fall in the 30 monthly complaints comes from prevention. This protects the $3.50 contribution on 120,000 units and the $900,000 investment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the quality options with minimal application to MPW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in MPW's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discussion of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why inspection and automation alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: MPW has a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership and 22 press operators needing digital-press training. Explain two benefits for MPW of introducing team working on the press floor.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working lets the 90 operators share knowledge about the 2.0% defect rate and the 30 monthly reprint complaints, so the 22 needing digital-press training learn from colleagues on the job. This spreads skills faster than top-down instructions from an autocratic leader and helps cut the 5.4% paper waste, protecting the $3.50 contribution per unit.

Point 2: Teams can solve small quality problems without waiting for decisions to travel through a hierarchical structure, shortening the 4.3-day turnaround that 71% of 520 managers value. Shared ownership also raises morale during the $900,000 press installation, reducing disruption to the 120,000-unit output and helping MPW meet national clients' deadlines.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of team working identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to MPW's complaints, waste and new press.

questions.question_text: MPW has 30 reprint complaints a month and 22 operators needing digital-press training. Consider paying bonuses for error-free work or funding external digital-press courses at $480 per employee. Which should MPW choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Bonus payments for error-free work: A financial motivator could focus the 90 operators on cutting the 2.0% defect rate and the 30 monthly reprint complaints, and bonuses are paid only when performance improves, so cost varies with results. It is simple to understand. However, bonuses do not teach the 22 staff how to use the new $900,000 press, and may encourage staff to hide errors rather than report them, which would leave the 5.4% paper waste unaddressed.

External digital-press courses at $480 per worker: Training all 22 operators costs 22 × $480 = $10,560, small beside the $900,000 press, and gives the skills needed to run the new machine and reduce reprints permanently. Certification also supports the 71% of 520 managers who value fast digital turnaround. The course takes staff off the floor, briefly slowing the 120,000-unit output and the 4.3-day turnaround, and generic content may need on-site follow-up.

Decision: MPW should fund the external digital-press courses, supported later by a modest error-free bonus. The root cause of 30 reprint complaints and 5.4% waste is a skills gap among 22 operators, which a bonus cannot fix; bonuses are rejected as they reward outcomes without building capability and may hide faults. Training is affordable at $10,560 and directly protects the $3.50 contribution and the $900,000 investment; a bonus can then reinforce the standards the trained staff set.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of bonuses and training with limited application to MPW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options in MPW's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a justified decision covering skills, cost and quality outcomes.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how the management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ ($7.30 − $3.80) = $300,000 ÷ $3.50 = 85,714.29 units. Answer: break-even output is 85,714.29 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $7.30 − $3.80 = $3.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $3.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MPW's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 85,714.29-unit break-even output with 120,000 units produced: the margin of safety is 34,285.71 units, showing how much demand can fall before the $300,000 fixed costs are uncovered.
2. Use the $3.50 contribution to test the $0.25 premium that 57% of managers would pay; raising $7.30 to $7.55 would lift contribution to $3.75, to be weighed against the 71% who value speed.
3. Use unit cost of $6.30 ($300,000 ÷ 120,000 = $2.50 plus $3.80 variable cost) to monitor the 5.4% paper waste and target the 2.0% defect rate.
4. Use labour productivity of about 1,333 units per worker (120,000 ÷ 90) to judge whether the 22 operators can be trained on the $900,000 press without disrupting the 4.3-day turnaround.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 85,714.29 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $3.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 34,285.71-unit margin of safety; $0.25 premium pricing; unit cost $6.30 to cut 5.4% waste; labour productivity about 1,333 units per worker for training plans.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MPW's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MPW's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.83 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.70 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.08 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $200,000 inventories + $140,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $375,000; 2025 current assets = $180,000 + $165,000 + $95,000 = $440,000. The 2024 liquidity comparison is $375,000 ÷ $250,000 = 1.50; the 2025 comparison is $440,000 ÷ $240,000 = 1.83. The stock-excluding measure for 2024 is ($375,000 − $200,000) ÷ $250,000 = $175,000 ÷ $250,000 = 0.70; for 2025 it is ($440,000 − $180,000) ÷ $240,000 = $260,000 ÷ $240,000 = 1.08.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved strongly. Current assets rose from $375,000 to $440,000 while current liabilities fell from $250,000 to $240,000, lifting the 2024 figure of 1.50 to 1.83 in 2025. The stock-excluding measure rose from 0.70 to 1.08, so MPW can now cover its short-term debts without selling the $180,000 of inventories — valuable while it services a $300,000 bank loan and has just raised $600,000 for the $900,000 press. Cash more than doubled from $35,000 to $95,000, a genuine improvement in headroom. Receivables did rise from $140,000 to $165,000, so some customers are slower to pay, but the cash increase more than offsets this. The 5.4% paper waste tied up in inventories is a smaller concern while stock is falling.

Conclusion: MPW's financial position has improved. Both measures (1.50 to 1.83 and 0.70 to 1.08) are higher, and the rise in cash confirms the gain is real rather than stock-driven. MPW should keep control of the $165,000 of receivables as the $900,000 press beds in.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or simple changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and liabilities and a justified conclusion on whether financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MPW of installing the new digital printing press.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The research shows 71% of 520 managers value fast digital turnaround and 57% would pay $0.25 more per unit, so MPW can shorten its 4.3-day turnaround and protect the $3.50 contribution per unit despite a 10.2% rise in paper and ink costs. Faster, more consistent printing also helps cut the 30 monthly reprint complaints and the 5.4% paper waste, supporting the $900,000 investment.

Disadvantage: The $900,000 capital cost is large and must be serviced alongside a $300,000 bank loan, while 22 of 90 operators need $480 training courses before the press runs efficiently. If digital output is lower than expected, the 85,714.29-unit break-even output may not be covered, and early technical faults could raise the 2.0% defect rate and delay national clients' orders.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to MPW's research, costs and investment.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.80%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in paper and ink costs will affect MPW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.80%): If MPW's $300,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.80% of $300,000 = $2,400 a year (0.008 × $300,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $300,000 a year, and a fixed-rate loan would see no increase. Higher rates may slow clients' marketing spend, but MPW can cap the risk by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.36 an hour): Some of the workforce of 90 is likely hourly-paid, so wage costs rise. The insert gives no hours worked or pay by role, so no annual wage bill can be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 120,000 units ÷ 90 workers = about 1,333 units per worker. If the $900,000 digital press lifts output per worker, the wage rise is affordable; if the 22 untrained operators and 5.4% waste hold productivity back, unit labour cost rises and the $3.50 contribution shrinks.

Paper and ink input costs (10.2%): These feed the $3.80 variable cost per unit, but the insert does not split it, so only a labelled bound is defensible: if the whole variable cost rose 10.2%, that is 10.2% × $3.80 = about $0.39 per unit; across 120,000 units that is roughly $46,800 a year (120,000 × $0.39). The 57% of managers who would pay $0.25 more offer partial recovery, but printing demand grew only 3.3%, so a full price rise may lose jobs.

Conclusion: The 10.2% paper and ink rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 120,000 units and directly erodes the $3.50 contribution that justifies the $900,000 press; the interest rise is a known $2,400 at most, and the wage rise can be offset by productivity gains from automation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to MPW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MPW's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes with a justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
